reading.body:
Education AI is tracked here through policy, market intelligence, and course listings, not through specific tools or infrastructure.

The four entries point to federal guidance for schools, a market-intelligence platform covering EdTech funding and AI learning platforms, and two references to a catalog of courses and credentials. The summary identifies tutoring systems, drafting assistance, and academic integrity policy as the live questions from K-12 through university. That pattern suggests the field is being defined by rules and training pathways more than by named deployments.

For AI scaling, this data offers no direct signal about compute, buildings, or power. It does not list data centers, energy demand, or hardware. What it does show is that education's AI footprint is currently administrative and pedagogical, with procurement and credentialing as the visible pressure points. Readers should not infer infrastructure constraints from this set.

analysis.body:
Per the Census Bureau, 30.0% of firms in Educational services (NAICS 61) answered yes to whether the business had used AI in the last two weeks, the latest figure in a series whose question was first asked in September 2023. The prior period stood at 35.5%. The survey note states that S means suppressed, so some cells are withheld rather than reported.

The Department of Education issued the federal guidance that anchors much of the public sector posture here. Its page describes an inventory of AI use-cases assembled to demonstrate the Department's commitment to AI innovation and advancement, and it names tools including CAISY, Grammarly's AI assistant, Otter.AI and AWS Bedrock. The stated purposes are decision-making and operational efficiency through real-time insights, predictive analytics and intelligent automation, written communication support, real-time transcription and collaboration for meetings, interviews and lectures, and building and scaling applications on foundation models for text generation, summarization, conversational AI, personalization and content creation. The same inventory is specific about routine work: AI generates summaries and outlines for projects and presentations, produces code snippets in a variety of programming languages, extracts key points and action items from publicly available documents, returns R code for data analysis, trains employees on prompt engineering, automates conversion between related data types such as translating a county name into its FIPS code, generates mock data sets for testing, drafts outreach strategies and project plans, and suggests descriptive paragraphs, workflow diagrams and qualifications for public positions. One listed use is testing filters and data loss prevention by feeding fabricated examples of prohibited prompt information.

On regulatory posture, the Department's OCIO supports adherence to federal regulations pertaining to AI advancement and responsible and secure usage, in accordance with the Executive Order Removing Barriers to American Leadership in Artificial Intelligence. That is the posture the page states, framed around innovation and risk management rather than restriction, and the risk material it surfaces is operational, meaning filter testing, data loss prevention and secure usage rather than a list of prohibited applications.

Courses and certifications are catalogued here tracks 13 AI courses, 11 of them free, 3 with public companion code, curated by level and audience with one verified source each and re-verified daily. Four are university graduate courses with public materials, Stanford's CS224n and CS231n, UC Berkeley's CS285 and MIT's 6.S191, while the rest come from industry, DeepLearning.AI, Google, Hugging Face, fast.ai and independent researcher Andrej Karpathy. The page describes university courses as generally structured around exam-driven theory and the industry courses as code-first or hands-on, and it states plainly that the data does not report enrollment numbers, completion rates, or which course is most widely taken. Membership is editorial, with nothing paid placement.

HolonIQ tracks the education economy as a market intelligence platform for the global impact economy, sizing addressable markets, quantifying demand and forecasting scenarios at varying rates of growth, and quantifying impact with rubrics, ratings and scoring to power policy, procurement and investment decisions. It describes mapping partnership and competitive landscapes and serving governments, institutions, technology companies, global firms and investors. The excerpts do not report education-specific funding totals or adoption rates, so nothing here should be read as a market size for AI in education.

For a reader deciding whether to deploy, the material supports a narrow set of conclusions. Measured adoption among educational services firms is real but not universal, at 30.0% in the latest Census figure, and it sits below the prior period's 35.5%. The Department of Education's own inventory shows that the deployments it documents are mostly back-office and instructional support tasks, summarization, drafting, transcription, code assistance and data preparation, with explicit attention to filter testing and data loss prevention. The course catalog shows where the skills are taught and notes that free access is common, but it does not report whether any of it changes outcomes. ROI evidence in these excerpts is limited to the Department's stated aims of reducing costs and boosting productivity, with no measured returns reported.

https://www.holoniq.com/.brief: HolonIQ describes itself as a platform that supplies data and research on the global impact economy. It offers tools for sizing markets, forecasting growth, and measuring impact through rubrics and ratings. The site also claims to provide competitive intelligence, partnership mapping, and strategic guidance for digital transformation. Users can receive newsletters with trending topics about impact, technology, and finance.

https://www.ed.gov/about/ed-overview/art.brief: The Department of Education's Office of the Chief Information Officer oversees the department's use of artificial intelligence in compliance with federal regulations and an executive order on AI leadership. The department has catalogued multiple AI applications across its operations, including tools for meeting transcription, writing assistance, code generation, data analysis, and document summarization. Additional uses include generating mock datasets for testing, automating data conversions, creating job descriptions, developing outreach strategies, and testing security filters. The guidance reflects the department's approach to balancing AI innovation with responsible and secure deployment.
